0.title: Words That Wound and Words That Heal
0.essay:
Most of us speak thousands of words a day, and type thousands more. We rarely stop to think how much they matter. Yet Scripture says, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs 18:21).

Words matter

A single sentence can crush a child’s spirit or lift a friend out of despair. Words can start wars, end marriages and destroy reputations. They can also bring comfort, peace and the good news of salvation.

Jesus said our words reveal our hearts: “For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34). And he warned that we will answer for them: “I tell you, on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak” (Matthew 12:36). That is sobering for anyone who has ever said something they regret — which is everyone.

On screens as well as lips

Everything in this study applies equally to emails, messages and social media, where many of today’s most careless words are written.

The chapters

The Power of Words; Sins of the Tongue; Words That Build Up; Speaking the Truth in Love; and Taming the Tongue — how God changes our speech by changing our hearts.

1.title: The Power of Words
1.essay:
The Bible opens with God speaking the world into existence: “And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light” (Genesis 1:3). God’s words create, command, promise and save. His Son is called the Word (John 1:1). And made in his image, we are speaking creatures, whose words carry a reflection of his creative power, for good or ill.

A small member with great power

James uses vivid pictures. The tongue is like a bit in a horse’s mouth or a rudder on a ship: small, but it steers the whole. It is like a spark in a forest: “How great a forest is set ablaze by such a small fire! And the tongue is a fire” (James 3:5–6). One careless remark can spread destruction far beyond what we intended. Few passages in Scripture describe a sin so vividly.

He begins with a warning to teachers: “Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness” (James 3:1). Those whose words reach many carry greater responsibility. Then he widens it to everyone: “For we all stumble in many ways. And if anyone does not stumble in what he says, he is a perfect man” (James 3:2).

Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, was asked by the people to lighten their burdens. The older advisers urged him to speak kindly; the younger urged harshness. He answered harshly, and ten tribes broke away (1 Kings 12:13–16). A few harsh words divided a nation.

Untameable by us

“For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature, can be tamed and has been tamed by mankind, but no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison” (James 3:7–8). We can train animals but not our own mouths. That is humbling, and it drives us to God.

Words reveal the heart

Jesus spoke to Pharisees who had just accused him of being in league with Satan. A tree is known by its fruit, he said, and a person by their words. “The good person out of his good treasure brings forth good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure brings forth evil” (Matthew 12:35). The tongue is not the root problem but the outflow. Harsh words come from a harsh heart, lying words from a deceitful heart, complaining words from a discontented heart. To change our speech, we need changed hearts.

“For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned” (Matthew 12:37). Our words are evidence of what is in us, and God hears every one, including those spoken in private or typed anonymously.

We reap what we speak

“From the fruit of a man’s mouth his stomach is satisfied; he is satisfied by the yield of his lips. Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruits” (Proverbs 18:20–21). Proverbs pictures words as food that comes back to fill us. What we say returns to us.

A father, frustrated after a long day, tells his teenage son, “You’ll never amount to anything.” He forgets it the next day. His son remembers it for twenty years. When the father finally realises, he asks his son’s forgiveness, and they both weep.

Blessing and cursing

James notes the strange inconsistency of the tongue: “With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so” (James 3:9–10). We sing praises on Sunday and speak cruelly at home on Monday. A spring does not pour out fresh and salt water; a fig tree does not bear olives. A consistent life produces consistent speech.

James grounds the rebuke in the image of God. To curse a human being is to dishonour his likeness. That is why insults, mockery and contempt are serious sins; Jesus said that whoever calls his brother a fool is liable to judgment (Matthew 5:22).

Words that save

The same tongue that can destroy can proclaim eternal life. God has chosen to save people through words, the preaching of the gospel: “How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching?” (Romans 10:14).

Think back over the words you spoke or wrote yesterday. Which did the most good? Which did the most harm?

For reflection

Why does James say no human being can tame the tongue? What do your words over the last week reveal about your heart? Can you remember words spoken to you that still affect you, for good or harm? How does the truth that you will give account for every careless word change how you speak?

2.title: Sins of the Tongue
2.essay:
Scripture names many sins of speech. Seeing them clearly helps us recognise them in ourselves.

Lying

“Therefore, having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbor, for we are members one of another” (Ephesians 4:25). Lying includes outright falsehood, half-truths, exaggeration and creating false impressions. Notice Paul’s reason: lying to a fellow believer is like one part of the body deceiving another. The devil “is a liar and the father of lies” (John 8:44). God is truth.

The ninth commandment — “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor” (Exodus 20:16) — forbids not only lying in court but every word that unjustly harms a neighbour’s reputation. It also calls us to defend others’ good names.

Gossip and slander

“Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets, but he who is trustworthy in spirit keeps a thing covered” (Proverbs 11:13). Gossip spreads private information to people who do not need it; slander spreads false or damaging information to harm someone’s reputation. Both destroy trust and divide friends. “For lack of wood the fire goes out, and where there is no whisperer, quarreling ceases” (Proverbs 26:20). Proverbs adds that gossip is like delicious food that goes down into the inner parts, and that smooth words can hide a hateful heart (Proverbs 26:22–25).

Christians sometimes spread gossip under cover of “prayer requests” or “concern”. Before sharing information about someone, ask: Is it true? Is it necessary? Is it kind? Would I say it in their presence?

Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses, partly over his wife and partly out of jealousy. God heard it and struck Miriam with leprosy — and Moses, the one wronged, prayed for her healing (Numbers 12:1–13). God takes slander of his servants seriously.

A group of church members often meet for coffee, and the conversation regularly turns to criticism of others. One woman realises she leaves every time feeling worse about her church. She decides to steer conversations elsewhere and, when necessary, to say gently, “I don’t think we should talk about her when she’s not here.” Others are relieved.

Harsh and angry words

“A harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1). Shouting, insulting and belittling words wound deeply, and Jesus taught that calling someone a fool in anger is a serious sin (Matthew 5:22).

Complaining and grumbling

“Do all things without grumbling or disputing, that you may be blameless and innocent, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and twisted generation, among whom you shine as lights in the world” (Philippians 2:14–15). Israel grumbled in the wilderness, and God took it as rebellion against him (Numbers 14:27). Constant complaining spreads discontent and shows a lack of trust in God’s goodness. A Christian who does not complain stands out; contentment in speech is itself a witness.

Flattery and boasting

“A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet” (Proverbs 29:5). Flattery is insincere praise used to manipulate, a kind of lying. Boasting — speaking to make ourselves look good, exaggerating our achievements or dropping names — comes from pride.

Crude talk

“Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving” (Ephesians 5:4). Coarse humour and obscene language dishonour God and cheapen what is precious.

Too many words

“When words are many, transgression is not lacking, but whoever restrains his lips is prudent” (Proverbs 10:19). Sometimes the sin is simply talking too much: not listening, and filling silence with careless words. The same chapter contrasts the fool, who hides hatred with lying lips and spreads slander, with the righteous: “The tongue of the righteous is choice silver … The lips of the righteous feed many” (Proverbs 10:20–21).

Online

Social media amplifies every sin of the tongue. Anonymity, speed and distance make people say things they would never say face to face. The same rules apply online as everywhere else.

Which sin of the tongue are you most prone to? Ask someone close to you; they probably know.

For reflection

Which of these sins are you most prone to? How do you tell sharing a concern from gossip? Why does Paul connect truthfulness to being “members one of another”? What would change in your online speech if you applied this chapter?

3.title: Words That Build Up
3.essay:
The tongue is not only dangerous. It is also one of the greatest instruments of good. The same mouth that can wound can heal.

Words that give grace

“Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Ephesians 4:29–30). “Corrupting” means rotten, spreading decay. Paul’s test for our words is threefold: do they build up? Do they fit the occasion? Do they give grace? Words can be channels of God’s grace to others. And our speech affects not only others but the Spirit who lives in us. Harsh words grieve him; gracious words please him.

Gentle answers

“A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger … A gentle tongue is a tree of life” (Proverbs 15:1, 4). In conflict, a gentle tone often calms what a sharp one would inflame. Our tone often matters as much as our words.

Encouragement

“Therefore encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing” (1 Thessalonians 5:11). Barnabas, whose name Acts says means “son of encouragement” (Acts 4:36), saw the good in people others doubted. When the newly converted Saul came to Jerusalem, the disciples were afraid of him. Barnabas took him, brought him to the apostles and vouched for him (Acts 9:26–27). A few words from Barnabas opened the door for the greatest missionary in history. Later he did the same for young John Mark.

Some believers have a particular gift of encouragement (Romans 12:8), but all are called to “exhort one another every day” (Hebrews 3:13). A teacher writes a short note to a struggling student, telling her she has a gift for writing. Years later that student, now an author, says the note was why she kept going. The teacher had forgotten writing it.

Kind and timely words

“Gracious words are like a honeycomb, sweetness to the soul and health to the body” (Proverbs 16:24). Kind words have physical, emotional and spiritual effects. “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver” (Proverbs 25:11). The right word at the right moment is a rare and beautiful gift.

Gratitude and blessing

Paul replaces crude talk with thanksgiving (Ephesians 5:4). Thanking God and thanking others changes the atmosphere of a home, a workplace or a church.

Scripture often speaks of blessing others with words. Parents blessed children; priests blessed the people: “The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you” (Numbers 6:24–25). Christians are called to “bless those who curse you” (Luke 6:28). Speaking blessing reflects the heart of God, who blesses.

Gospel words

The greatest words we can speak are words about Christ. “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!” (Romans 10:15). Every Christian can speak of what Christ has done for them.

“Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (Colossians 4:5–6). Our conversations with unbelievers are opportunities. Gracious speech is not bland; salt gives flavour and preserves. Christian speech should be kind, thoughtful and interesting.

The model of Christ

In Nazareth people “marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth” (Luke 4:22). Jesus spoke truth with perfect grace. He knew when to rebuke and when to comfort, when to speak and when to be silent.

Who could you encourage today with a specific, sincere word?

For reflection

Apply Paul’s threefold test from Ephesians 4:29 to a recent conversation. Who has spoken words of encouragement that shaped your life? How could you speak more gratitude in your home or workplace? What does it mean for your speech to be “seasoned with salt”?

4.title: Speaking the Truth in Love
4.essay:
Two errors are common in Christian speech. Some speak truth without love: they are blunt, critical and harsh, and they call it honesty. Others speak love without truth: they flatter, avoid hard conversations and never say anything difficult, and they call it kindness. Paul calls us to something better: “speaking the truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15).

How churches grow up

God gives the church teachers to equip believers for ministry, so that it grows to maturity and is not “tossed to and fro by the waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine” (Ephesians 4:14). The means of growth is speaking the truth in love, so that “we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ” (Ephesians 4:15). Every member contributes. Healthy churches are places of honest, loving conversation, not flattery or harshness.

Truth matters

God hates lying, and love does not pretend. “Better is open rebuke than hidden love. Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy” (Proverbs 27:5–6). A friend who never tells us hard truths is not really a friend. Flatterers tell us what we want to hear, perhaps because they do not care. Nathan’s rebuke to David — “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7) — was an act of love that led to repentance.

Love matters

Truth without love is a weapon. “There is one whose rash words are like sword thrusts, but the tongue of the wise brings healing” (Proverbs 12:18). Love chooses the right time, place, tone and words. It speaks privately before publicly. It speaks to help, not to win. “Truthful lips endure forever, but a lying tongue is but for a moment … Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who act faithfully are his delight” (Proverbs 12:19, 22).

Correction should be gentle, humble and aimed at restoration: “if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness” (Galatians 6:1). Jesus gives a pattern for addressing sin: privately first, then with one or two others, then with the church (Matthew 18:15–17). Most conflicts should be resolved at the first step, with honest, gentle speech.

Christ joined them perfectly

Jesus spoke hard truths to the Pharisees, to Peter and to the rich young ruler. But Mark says of the rich young man, “And Jesus, looking at him, loved him” (Mark 10:21), before telling him what he needed to hear. Truth and love were perfectly joined in Christ.

Listening first

“Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God” (James 1:19–20). Many conflicts would be avoided if we listened carefully before speaking. “If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and shame” (Proverbs 18:13). And James goes straight on to receiving God’s word “with meekness” (James 1:21). Listening to God and listening to others go together.

Receiving truth

Speaking the truth in love also means receiving it. Humble Christians welcome correction, even when it stings. “Let a righteous man strike me—it is a kindness; let him rebuke me—it is oil for my head; let my head not refuse it” (Psalm 141:5).

When Peter, under pressure, withdrew from eating with Gentile believers, Paul “opposed him to his face” (Galatians 2:11). It was a hard conversation, but the gospel was at stake. Years later Peter wrote of “our beloved brother Paul” (2 Peter 3:15). Truth spoken in love did not end their friendship.

A turning point

A woman notices that her friend has become bitter and sharp-tongued since a family conflict. She is tempted to say nothing. Instead she prays, chooses a quiet moment and says, “I love you, and I’m worried. Can I share something I’ve noticed?” Her friend is hurt at first, then grateful. It becomes a turning point.

For reflection

Do you tend more toward truth without love, or love without truth? How can you grow? Is there a hard but loving conversation you have been avoiding? How well do you receive correction? Which of James 1:19’s three — quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger — is hardest for you?

5.title: Taming the Tongue
5.essay:
If no human being can tame the tongue (James 3:8), is there any hope? Yes — because God can. He changes our speech by changing our hearts.

A new heart

Jesus repeats the principle: “The good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure produces evil, for out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks” (Luke 6:45). To change our words, God must change our hearts. And he does.

Cleansed lips

When Isaiah saw the holy God, he became aware at once of his own unclean lips and his people’s: “Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5). A seraph touched his mouth with a burning coal from the altar, the place of sacrifice, and said, “Behold, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for” (Isaiah 6:7). Then Isaiah was ready to speak for God. Cleansed lips come from atonement. Ours are cleansed by the sacrifice of Christ, and the more we treasure him, the more our words will reflect him.

Every Christian has sinned with the tongue countless times, and Christ’s blood covers those sins too. We fight sins of speech not to earn forgiveness but because we have received it.

Prayer for our speech

“Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips! Do not let my heart incline to any evil” (Psalm 141:3–4). Guarding the tongue begins with prayer and humility; in the same breath David welcomes rebuke from the righteous as a kindness.

David ends his great psalm about God’s word with a prayer to be kept from hidden faults and presumptuous sins, and then: “Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, O LORD, my rock and my redeemer” (Psalm 19:14). Words that please God come from a heart shaped by his word. Praying before conversations, meetings and difficult phone calls invites his help.

Filled with the word

“Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly” (Colossians 3:16). When Scripture fills our hearts, it shapes our words. Memorising Scripture gives us better things to say.

And the Spirit produces new speech. Self-control, gentleness and kindness are his fruit (Galatians 5:22–23). We cooperate by putting off the old and putting on the new.

The value of silence

“Even a fool who keeps silent is considered wise; when he closes his lips, he is deemed intelligent” (Proverbs 17:28). “Whoever keeps his mouth and his tongue keeps himself out of trouble” (Proverbs 21:23). Sometimes the most godly thing we can do is say nothing. Waiting before replying, especially in anger or online, prevents many sins.

Confession and repair

When we sin with our words, we should confess quickly, to God and to those we have hurt: “I was wrong to say that. Will you forgive me?” Words that wounded can be followed by words that heal.

Practical habits

Pause before speaking when angry. Do not send a message written in anger until you have slept on it. Before passing on news about someone, ask whether it is true, necessary and kind. Speak about people as if they were present. Look for one person to encourage each day.

A man known for his sharp tongue at work starts praying Psalm 141:3 every morning. He also makes a rule: when he feels angry in a meeting, he waits ten seconds before speaking. Over months colleagues notice the change, and one asks him what happened. He tells her about Christ.

Peter’s tongue

Peter’s tongue got him into trouble again and again: rebuking Jesus, boasting that he would never deny him, then denying him with curses (Mark 8:32; 14:29, 71). After Pentecost, filled with the Spirit, the same tongue preached Christ boldly to thousands (Acts 2). God tamed Peter’s tongue and used it.

Perfect speech

“If anyone does not stumble in what he says, he is a perfect man” (James 3:2). No one achieves that in this life. But in glory our speech will be perfectly holy. Every word will praise God and bless others, and the redeemed will sing a new song to the Lamb (Revelation 5:9).

What one practical habit could you adopt this week to guard your tongue?

For reflection

Pray Psalm 141:3 and Psalm 19:14 each morning this week: what difference does it make? When is silence the wisest response for you? Is there someone you need to ask forgiveness for words you spoke? How does Isaiah 6:5–7 show where clean speech comes from?
